scenarios.title: The Kicker You Watched Retire
scenarios.text: A kicker you watched as a kid has a statue unveiled outside his old stadium, and you're invited to speak. You still have his rookie card in a shoebox somewhere, bent at one corner.

choices.label: Speak about the kid you were
choices.result: A speech about the kid in front of a television, copying his steps in the backyard. He hears it from the front row, and hugs you afterwards for a long time.

choices.label: Bring the bent card
choices.result: The bent rookie card, brought along in your jacket pocket and handed to him to sign. He laughs at the corner and signs it anyway, and you frame it at home.

choices.label: Ask him how he stopped
choices.result: Over coffee after the ceremony, a question about how he knew it was time to stop. His answer is short, and it's the most useful thing anyone has told you this year.

scenarios.title: The Night Practice
scenarios.text: A night practice at your age, under the lights in the cold, and the chill gets into your joints in a way it never used to. The young players are in shorts, and you're wearing two jackets.

choices.label: Warm up twice as long
choices.result: Twice the warmup, on purpose, while the young players tease you about it. You kick clean for the whole session, and they stop teasing when they see the chart.

choices.label: Kick in the jackets
choices.result: Both jackets on, through the whole practice, looking ridiculous. It works, the young players start calling it 'veteran style', and two of them copy it the next week.

choices.label: Ask to skip the late reps
choices.result: A quiet word with the special teams coach about skipping the last reps. He agrees immediately, and your joints thank you in the morning.

scenarios.title: The New Recovery Tech
scenarios.text: The club has bought new recovery technology: a cold chamber that looks like a phone booth from the future. The trainers want you to try it first, because if it helps you, it'll help anyone.

choices.label: Go in first
choices.result: Three minutes in the chamber, in shorts and gloves, while the young players film it. You come out shaking and laughing, and your hip feels better than it has in weeks.

choices.label: Read the research first
choices.result: The research, read on a Sunday afternoon before you agree. It's mixed and interesting, and you use the chamber twice a week instead of every day.

choices.label: Stick with what works
choices.result: No thanks: the old ice bath has worked for years, and you're not changing now. The trainers shrug, and the young players start calling the ice bath 'classic'.

scenarios.title: The Gala in Your Honor
scenarios.text: A charity gala honors your career while you're still playing: a ballroom, a video tribute, a table of old coaches, and a speech expected from you after dessert.

choices.label: Give the speech
choices.result: A speech about the people at the coaches' table, one by one. The ballroom goes quiet, and three of the coaches have to look at the ceiling for a while.

choices.label: Ask the old coaches to speak
choices.result: Your speech time handed to the old coaches, who tell stories about you that you'd rather forget. The room laughs for twenty minutes, and the night raises twice the goal.

choices.label: Keep it to a toast
choices.result: A toast, short and sincere, and then you sit down and let the evening belong to the charity. The organizers say it was perfect, and the kids it helps get their camp.

choices.label: Hand the night to your foundation's kids
choices.result: The kids from your own foundation come up on stage instead of you and tell the ballroom what it did for them. There isn't a dry eye anywhere, including yours.

scenarios.title: The Retirement Present
scenarios.text: Your teammates buy you a retirement present before you've retired: a rocking chair with your number painted on the back, presented in the locker room with a speech from the youngest player.

choices.label: Sit in it for the meeting
choices.result: You carry the rocking chair into the special teams meeting and rock through the whole thing. The coaches can't keep a straight face, and the young players love it.

choices.label: Thank them properly
choices.result: A real thank-you, to the youngest player first, and then to the room. You say more than you planned about what they've meant, and nobody makes a joke after.

choices.label: Promise to use it later
choices.result: A promise: the chair goes on your porch when you're done, and not a day before. Until then it lives in your locker as a reminder, and a dare.

scenarios.title: The Last Contract Signing
scenarios.text: You sign what everyone assumes is your last contract: one year, a fair number, and a general manager who shakes your hand for a beat longer than usual and says 'Enjoy it.'

choices.label: Enjoy it, like he said
choices.result: You take his advice and enjoy it: every practice, every flight, every stupid joke in the locker room. It turns into one of the happiest seasons of your career.

choices.label: Treat it like any other
choices.result: Business as usual: the routine, the film, the early mornings. You'll know when it's the last, and it isn't the contract's job to tell you.

choices.label: Take the family to dinner
choices.result: A dinner with family and old friends the night of the signing, at the place from your rookie year. The waiter remembers you, and the stories run past midnight.

scenarios.title: The Long Snapper's Retirement
scenarios.text: The long snapper you've worked with for years is retiring. He tells you in the parking lot after practice, before anyone else, and then stands there jingling his keys, waiting for you to say something.

choices.label: Say the true thing
choices.result: The true thing, said in the parking lot: you couldn't have done any of it without him. He nods, looks away, and drives off honking his horn twice.

choices.label: Throw him a send-off
choices.result: A send-off at his favorite diner with every specialist he's ever worked with. Some of them fly in, and the diner has to close early to fit them all.

choices.label: Ask him to coach the new one
choices.result: A request: stay around for camp and coach his replacement. He agrees, grumbling, and the new snapper is better by August than anyone expected.

scenarios.title: The Rival's Kid
scenarios.text: {tyler}'s kid is a kicker in college now, and {tyler} has sent you film with a short note: tell me honestly, is there anything there? The kid has your old plant foot, which is either a compliment or a curse.

choices.label: Tell the truth
choices.result: The honest answer, written carefully: real talent, one big flaw, and a lot of work ahead. {tyler} thanks you, and says it's what they needed to hear from someone else.

choices.label: Fix the plant foot
choices.result: A video message for the kid, showing how you fixed the same plant foot years ago. The kid fixes it in a month, and {tyler} sends you a photo of the chart.

choices.label: Invite the kid to train
choices.result: A weekend of training together in the summer, offered by video message. The kid comes, nervous and polite, and {tyler} watches from the bleachers, saying nothing at all.

scenarios.title: The Old College Coach's Funeral
scenarios.text: The coach who brought you to college has died. The family has asked former players to speak at the service, and the list of names on the program is long and familiar.

choices.label: Speak at the service
choices.result: A few minutes at the lectern, about the day he came to your house and sat at the kitchen table. His widow holds your hand afterwards and doesn't let go for a while.

choices.label: Sit with the old teammates
choices.result: No speech, just a pew with your old college teammates, shoulder to shoulder. Afterwards you all go to the old diner near campus and tell his stories until closing.

choices.label: Write to the family
choices.result: A long letter to his family, about the things he taught you that had nothing to do with kicking. They read it at the reception, and his grandson asks to meet you.

choices.label: Tell them about the night he picked you up
choices.result: The story of the night he drove across town to pick you up from a party you'd left early, without a single question. His family had never heard it, and they laugh and cry at once.
choices.lock_text: having left the party early in college

scenarios.title: The Weight You Can't Lose
scenarios.text: You can't keep the weight off the way you used to. The scale in the training room has become an enemy, and the nutritionist has started leaving recipes in your locker with sticky notes on them.

choices.label: Follow the recipes
choices.result: Every recipe, cooked on Sunday and eaten all week, sticky notes and all. It's dull, and by October the scale has stopped being an enemy and gone back to being a scale.

choices.label: Add one more workout
choices.result: One more workout a week, early on Saturdays, on the bike. It's hard on old legs, and it works, slowly, and the nutritionist sends a smiley face.

choices.label: Make peace with the scale
choices.result: Peace with the scale: a few pounds at your age is fine if the leg still works. The trainers agree, the stress goes away, and you eat dinner happily again.

scenarios.title: The Sleep You Need
scenarios.text: You need ten hours of sleep now, and road trips don't allow it: late flights, early meetings, hotel rooms with curtains that don't close. The trainer has started tracking your sleep on a watch.

choices.label: Ask for a quieter room
choices.result: A quiet word with the travel staff: a room at the end of the hall, blackout tape and an earlier flight when possible. They manage it most weeks, and you feel human again.

choices.label: Nap like a professional
choices.result: Naps, planned like workouts: on the plane, on the bus, in the training room before meetings. The young players laugh until they try it themselves.

choices.label: Push through
choices.result: Pushing through, the way you always have. You're tired all season, and the watch's reports become a running joke between you and the trainer.

scenarios.title: The Young Coach's Respect
scenarios.text: A young coach on the staff admits, after practice, that he learned to coach kickers by watching your film when he was in college. He has notes from your games in an old binder, with arrows and question marks.

choices.label: Go through the binder together
choices.result: An evening with the binder, answering every question mark he wrote years ago. Some of his guesses were right, and some were wildly wrong, and you both laugh at those.

choices.label: Ask what he'd change now
choices.result: A question back: what would he change in your kick today? His answer is sharp and useful, and it goes into your routine the next morning.

choices.label: Sign the binder
choices.result: A signature on the binder's cover, with a note about the question marks. He keeps it on his desk for the rest of his career and shows it to every young kicker he coaches.

scenarios.title: The Media's Last Questions
scenarios.text: Every press conference now ends with the same question about retirement, and you've started to feel the reporters waiting for it like a punchline. This week someone brought a stopwatch to time how long it takes.

choices.label: Answer before they ask
choices.result: You open the press conference by answering the retirement question first, with a straight face. The room laughs, the stopwatch reporter stops the clock, and the questions get better.

choices.label: Give the same answer every week
choices.result: The same answer, word for word, every week, until it becomes a catchphrase. By the end of the season the reporters say it with you, which is oddly warm.

choices.label: Talk to them off the record
choices.result: An off-the-record coffee with the regular reporters, about what it's really like. They ease off after that, and two of them write the kindest pieces of your career.
